CSCP Learning System 2024 · Module 5 · Forward and Reverse Logistics

How Much Warehouse Space Do You Need?

A step-by-step method for forecasting warehouse capacity: from average inventory, to pallet bays, to the square meters you would lease or build, with a worked example and an interactive calculator.

Source: APICS/ASCM CSCP Learning System 2024 (v5.2), Module 5 Section: Internal Warehouse Design and Capacity Forecasting Format: study summary in original wording
Summary 1 · Why forecast 2 · What to forecast 3 · Prepare inputs 4 · Seven steps 5 · Calculator 6 · What moves the answer 7 · Layout 8 · Variations Key terms Discussion
The short version

Five ideas to remember

01

Plan three to five years ahead. Space is a large capital commitment, and changing it sooner rarely pays.

02

Size for the typical level. Forecast average (mode) inventory, unless items have fixed locations, which need their maximum space.

03

Convert in stages. Volume to pallet bays, bays to floor area, then adjust for movement space, height, and spare capacity.

04

Derive factors from your own sites. The module's multipliers come from analyzing existing warehouses with similar equipment.

05

Utilization is a policy choice. The target comes from strategic and risk analysis, and it sets how much room you keep in reserve.

3–5 yearsforecast horizon; the highest-demand year sets the requirement
10,000 → 11,000pallet bays before and after the partial-pallet factor (module example)
13,200 m²raw floor footprint of the inventory alone (module example)
× 3 or moretypical multiplier for aisles, equipment, and handling space
12,375 m²final requirement in the module's worked example
1
Why forecast capacity

Decide the size before you build or lease

Warehouse capacity forecasting is a must before building or leasing space, because the facility needs enough capacity for the next three to five years.

Changing warehouse capacity over a shorter time frame tends not to be cost-effective. The module names the reasons: building and setup expense, and lease negotiations. Warehouse space is also a large capital investment, so it has to hold as much storage as possible while still leaving room for equipment movement and the other activities that happen inside it.

  • Receiving and cross-docking
  • Order picking
  • Assembly and packaging
  • Staging for outbound shipment

The answer is finally expressed in square meters or square feet, because that is how real estate is sold or leased.

Where this fitsThe method answers one question: "How much floor space must this warehouse have to hold the forecasted inventory?" It sits inside the module's discussion of internal warehouse design, after layout and stock-location choices and before materials-handling equipment.
2
What to forecast

The most common inventory level, not the peak

Capacity forecasting is a function of aggregate inventory levels. Individual inventories move between a minimum (the safety stock) and a maximum, and the planning figure is the most common level in between.

The module calls that most common level the mode, and says it sits roughly halfway between the safety stock level and the maximum level. For the rest of the method, "average inventory" means this mode.

Sizing to the average can look like it leaves too little room for the maximum. With random-location storage it does not, because items that are currently at their maximum are balanced by items that are currently at their minimum.

The location method changes the answer

Random-location storage (floating)

Parts go into any empty space when they arrive. A locator file is needed to know where things are.

  • Often requires less storage space
  • Maximizes cube utilization
  • Can be rapid with directed pick and put-away automation
  • Size to the average (mode)

Fixed-location storage

Each item has a relatively permanent location. Locations become familiar, so a locator file may not be needed.

  • Needs more space than random-location
  • Acceptable where space is not at a premium, throughput is low, or there are few SKUs
  • Often used for slow-moving items such as spare parts
  • Size to the sum of every item's maximum space; expect much unused space
3
Prepare the inputs

Six things to settle before the arithmetic

The module lists a few points to handle before calculating the forecasted average inventory level. Skipping them is how a clean calculation gives the wrong answer.
1

Average by unit type, then aggregate

Calculate averages per type of unit. Items of similar size can be grouped by storage requirement, because the total cubic meters or feet is what matters.

2

Estimate what fits on a pallet

Count items per pallet, including how high it can be stacked. In practice, simplify from cubic volume to the number of pallet storage bays.

3

Standardize the pallet

Many organizations use one pallet size so any pallet fits any bay. Then each pallet counts as one unit.

4

Allow for partial pallets

A pallet that can hold 18 boxes but holds one still takes a whole bay, so a compensation factor is added.

5

Keep bulk separate

Any bulk storage requirement is calculated on its own.

6

Forecast every year, take the peak

Run the forecast for each of the three to five years. The year with the highest requirement sets the capacity, in cubic meters, cubic feet, or bays.

What this method does not doThe module takes the forecasted average inventory as a given input. How to forecast that figure (from the demand plan, safety stock, and replenishment policy) is a separate step, and the quality of the result depends on it.
4
The seven steps

From cubic meters to square meters

The module's worked example takes 18,000 cubic meters of average inventory in the peak forecast year and ends at 12,375 square meters of floor space.
Phase A

From volume to pallet bays

1

Take the peak-year average inventory volume

The sum of all forecasted average inventories in the highest year of a five-year plan.

18,000 m³module example
2

Convert volume to storage bays

Divide by the volume of one full standard pallet: 1.2 m deep × 1.0 m wide × 1.5 m tall = 1.8 m³.

18,000 ÷ 1.8
10,000 baysbefore adjustment
3

Compensate for partially filled pallets

Multiply by a factor based on historical analysis of existing warehouse usage (1.1 in the example).

10,000 × 1.1
11,000 baysneeded
Phase B

From bays to floor area

4

Determine the raw space footprint

Multiply bays by the floor area of one pallet (1.2 m × 1.0 m = 1.2 m²). Height is handled later.

11,000 × 1.2
13,200 m²inventory only
5

Add space for all movement

Multiply by a factor above one for the space around inventory in each bay, aisles, handling equipment, and picking, sorting, and consolidating. The module says this is typically at least three.

13,200 × 3
39,600 m²gross, single level
6

Account for vertical storage

Divide by the number of storage levels (four in the example: ground plus pallet racks three levels high).

39,600 ÷ 4
9,900 m²floor space
7

Build in expansion or spare capacity

Divide by the target utilization. At 80%, the warehouse is only 80% full under current forecasts.

9,900 ÷ 0.8
12,375 m²requirement

How the floor-area figure evolves

All seven steps in one expression

Floor area = (V ÷ Vp) × fp × Ap × fmL × U
V peak-year average inventory volume
Vp volume of one full pallet
fp partial-pallet factor
Ap floor area of one pallet
fm movement-space factor
L number of storage levels
U target utilization (e.g., 0.80)

The module presents the steps in sequence, not as one formula. The expression above is a consolidation made for this summary; it gives the same result as the steps (12,375 m² for the example).

7
Layout context

Why the movement factor is so large

Racks give cube utilization, but a warehouse that is only racks does not work. The movement factor exists because inventory shares the building with receiving, picking, packing, and staging flows.

Warehouses are generally designed as one-floor systems. Rack storage raises cube utilization (use of the building's cubic space) by storing items on vertical racks, and the maximum height is set by the equipment that places and picks pallets or by the building's height limit.

Filling an entire warehouse with single selective racks (multi-level racks one pallet deep on each side of an aisle) might store the most, but the workflow areas become congested and throughput could be "abysmal." A velocity analysis helps optimize flow, and the ideal is 100 percent accessibility: every pallet reachable without first moving another.

Cross-docking moves freight straight from receiving to outgoing shipping. The design aims to maximize dock space and minimize movement inside the building.

8
Variations and cautions

When the standard method needs adjusting

The module states plainly that there are many ways to determine warehouse space capacity. This is one, and these are the adjustments it names.

Fixed-location storage

Use maximum inventory requirements, not average, so you do not run out of space when orders arrive.

Volume split across several DCs

Divide the volume of goods per warehouse first, then run the remaining adjustments separately for each. The total is larger, because each warehouse needs its own functional areas for goods handling.

Where the factors come from

The movement factor should be found by analyzing existing warehouses that use the same types of equipment. The partial-pallet factor comes from historical analysis of existing warehouse usage.

Where the utilization target comes from

It is set by organizational policy, based on strategic and risk analyses. It is the module's way of building in excess capacity.

Bulk storage

Calculate any bulk storage capacity requirement separately from the pallet-bay calculation.

Height has to be real

The level count in step 6 only works if the building and the handling equipment can actually reach that height. The module notes maximum height is set by equipment or existing height limits.

The land or building you could acquireThe result can be read as the amount of land to lease or buy to build a new warehouse, or the size of an existing warehouse (with enough vertical height for the racks) to lease or purchase.
9
Key terms

Terms at a glance

TermPlain-language meaning
Mode (average inventory)The most common inventory level, roughly halfway between safety stock and the maximum; the planning figure in this method
Safety stockThe minimum level individual inventories fall to
Random-location storageParts go in any empty space on arrival; a locator file is needed; often needs less space
Fixed-location storageEach item has a relatively permanent location; needs more space; sized to maximums
Storage bayThe space for one standard pallet; the unit the calculation simplifies to
Partial-pallet factorA multiplier because a part-filled pallet still takes a whole bay
Raw space footprintBays × floor area per pallet, before movement space and height
Movement-space factorA multiplier for space around inventory, aisles, equipment, and picking, sorting, and consolidating
Cube utilizationHow much of the building's cubic space is used for storage, raised by vertical racks
Target utilizationThe planned share of space in use; dividing by it builds in spare capacity
Single selective rackMulti-level racking one pallet deep on each side of an aisle
Cross-dockingMoving freight directly from receiving to outbound shipping
Velocity analysisStudy of item movement speed used to optimize warehouse flow
100% accessibilityEvery pallet can be reached without first moving another
10
For discussion

Six reflection questions for your organization

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

Drawn from this section as material for team discussion. Answers depend on each organization's situation and should be backed by data rather than perception.

  1. Horizon. Does your capacity plan cover every year of a three-to-five-year forecast, and is the peak year the one used for sizing?
  2. Which level? Are you sizing to average inventory or to maximum, and does that match whether items are stored in random or fixed locations?
  3. Unit of measure. Have items been grouped by storage requirement and converted to pallet bays, and which items are bulk and calculated separately?
  4. Evidence for the factors. Where do your partial-pallet and movement factors come from: measured data from existing sites with similar equipment, or assumption?
  5. Utilization policy. What target utilization applies, and which strategic and risk analysis supports it?
  6. Network design. If volume is split across several sites, has each site been given its own handling and functional areas?
